note: Bar Haddaya was to deliver a bill of divorce from one country to another and asked Rabbi Ahai, who was in charge of bills of divorce, how to proceed. Rabbi Ahai told him he had to stand over every single letter as it was written. Bar Haddaya then asked Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, who told him he did not need to. The answer goes on: if he chose to be strict anyway, he would be casting doubt on the bills of divorce delivered before.
why: The Gemara has been discussing the agent's declaration that a bill of divorce was written and signed in his presence; this case asks how closely he must actually watch the writing to make it.

people.name: Bar Haddaya
people.about: An agent about to deliver a bill of divorce.

people.name: Rabbi Ahai
people.about: The Sage in charge of bills of divorce, who demands strict supervision.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: One of two Sages who tell Bar Haddaya he need not watch every letter.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: One of two Sages who tell Bar Haddaya he need not watch every letter.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage. When one is delivered from abroad, the agent who brings it must declare: It was written in my presence and signed in my presence.

note: Rabba bar bar Hana brought a bill of divorce, half of which had been written in his presence and half not. He asked Rabbi Elazar, who told him that if the scribe wrote even one line of it for the woman's sake in his presence, nothing more was needed. Rav Ashi said that even hearing the sound of the quill and the parchment is enough.
why: This continues the question of how much of the writing an agent must witness to declare that a bill of divorce was written in his presence; the teaching cited next is brought as support for Rav Ashi.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: An agent who saw only half of a bill of divorce being written.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: The Sage who tells him one line written in his presence is enough.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who says even hearing the writing is enough.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage. When one is delivered from abroad, the agent who brings it must declare: It was written in my presence and signed in my presence.
A bill of divorce must be written specifically for this woman, not prepared as a blank form.

note: Rav Hanin reports that Rav Kahana brought a bill of divorce, either from Sura to Neharde'a or the other way round; Rav Hanin did not know which. Rav Kahana asked Rav whether he had to declare: It was written in my presence and signed in my presence. Rav told him he did not have to.
why: The Gemara has been asking how far a bill of divorce must travel before the agent has to make this declaration; in the lines that follow, Rav's answer goes on to say that making it anyway protects the divorce if the husband contests it.

people.name: Rav Hanin
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: An agent bringing a bill of divorce.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage Rav Kahana asks.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage. When one is delivered from abroad, the agent who brings it must declare: It was written in my presence and signed in my presence.
Two Jewish towns in Babylonia.

flag: The story stops mid-sentence: Rav's answer continues in the next segment ('but if you do, you provide benefit').

note: A man brought a bill of divorce before Rabbi Yishmael and asked whether he had to declare that it was written and signed in his presence. Rabbi Yishmael asked where he was from, and on hearing 'the village of Sisai', told him to make the declaration, so that he would not need witnesses. After the man left, Rabbi Elai objected that Sisai lies within the Land of Israel, closer to Tzippori than Akko is, so the declaration was not needed. Rabbi Yishmael told him: Be silent, my son, be silent; since the matter went out as permitted, it went out.
why: The Gemara has just explained that an agent who makes the declaration even when not required means the husband's later challenge is ignored; this incident is cited as the source.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: The Sage who tells the man to make the declaration.

people.name: Rabbi Elai
people.about: A Sage who questions why the declaration was needed.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage. When one is delivered from abroad, the agent who brings it must declare: It was written in my presence and signed in my presence.
A city at the edge of the Land of Israel; Rabbi Meir rules it counts as the Land of Israel for bills of divorce.
A city in the heart of the Land of Israel.

note: Rabbi Evyatar met Elijah the prophet and asked him what God was doing. Elijah said God was studying the story of the concubine in Gibeah, saying: Evyatar My son says this, and Yonatan My son says that. Rabbi Evyatar protested: God forbid, is there uncertainty before Heaven? Elijah answered that both are the words of the living God: the husband found a fly and did not take offense, then found a hair and did.
why: Rabbi Evyatar's standing as a Sage has just been questioned, and Abaye defends him by saying God agreed with his reading; this meeting with Elijah is the proof.

people.name: Rabbi Evyatar
people.about: A Sage who asks Elijah what God is doing.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who reports what God is studying.

people.name: God
people.about: Described as studying the passage and quoting both Sages.

people.name: Yonatan
people.about: The Sage whose opposing reading God also quotes.

terms.meaning: The story in Judges 19 of a woman who left her husband, which led to a terrible war; the Sages disputed what had angered him.

terms.term: these and those are the words of the living God
terms.meaning: Both opinions are true; here, both incidents happened.

note: Rabbi Abbahu warns that a person should never impose excessive fear on his household, because a great man once did and his household fed him something carrying a grave prohibition. The Gemara names the man as Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel, then objects that God would not let a righteous man eat forbidden food. So, the Gemara explains, they only tried to feed him a limb cut from a living animal: one day his meat was missing a limb, and his frightened household cut one from a live animal to make the meal look whole, and he almost ate it.
why: The discussion has just quoted Rav that a man who terrifies his household will end up in serious sins, and that household instructions on Shabbat eve must be given calmly. Rabbi Abbahu's account is a concrete case of that danger.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: The Sage who gives the warning and tells the story.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel
people.about: The 'great man' whose household feared him so much that they nearly fed him forbidden meat.

terms.meaning: Meat cut from an animal while it is still alive. Eating it is forbidden to all people, and the Gemara counts it a grave prohibition.

note: Mar Ukva, the Exilarch (head of the Jewish community) in Babylonia, wrote to Rabbi Elazar in the Land of Israel: people were tormenting him, and he had the power to hand them over to the government. May he? Rabbi Elazar answered with a verse about keeping a curb on one's mouth while the wicked stand before you. Mar Ukva wrote again that the torment was too much to bear. Rabbi Elazar answered: be silent before the Lord, and He will strike them down; go early and stay late at the study hall, and they will disappear on their own. Soon after, Geneiva, Mar Ukva's tormentor, was put in a neck iron by the government.
why: The Gemara has been talking about letters sent from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and the scoring of lines on parchment before writing a verse; Rabbi Elazar's replies are such letters. The next passages pick up the theme of staying silent and leaving judgment to God.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: The Exilarch in Babylonia, who is being tormented and asks whether he may hand his tormentors to the government.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage in the Land of Israel who answers Mar Ukva's letters with verses.

people.name: Geneiva
people.about: Mar Ukva's tormentor, who ends up in a neck iron.

terms.meaning: Drew faint guide lines on the parchment before writing. Writing verses from the Bible required this.
An iron collar put on a prisoner condemned by the government.

note: The Exilarch, head of the Babylonian Jewish community, asked Rav Huna where the ban on putting a garland on a bridegroom's head comes from. Rav Huna said it is a rabbinic rule, decreed during Vespasian's war. When Rav Huna stepped out to relieve himself, his student Rav Ḥisda, who had kept silent out of respect, offered a verse from Ezekiel: remove the mitre and take off the garland. He explained that once the High Priest's mitre was gone, the bridegroom's garland went too. Rav Huna came back, found them discussing it, and swore by God that the ban is only rabbinic, but praised Rav Ḥisda with a pun on his name: your name is Ḥisda and your words find favor.
why: The discussion has turned to the mourning customs after the Temple's destruction: Mar Ukva has just ruled that song is forbidden. The question of wedding garlands is another such custom, and the verse Rav Ḥisda finds is taken up again in what follows.

people.name: The Exilarch
people.about: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who asks the question.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage and Rav Ḥisda's teacher, who says the ban on garlands is rabbinic.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Rav Huna's student, who speaks up only once his teacher has left the room.

terms.meaning: A rule made by the Sages, as opposed to one written in the Torah itself.
The turban worn by the High Priest in the Temple.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses and quotes.

note: Ravina came upon Mar bar Rav Ashi braiding a garland for his daughter's wedding. Ravina asked him whether he did not hold by the verse 'Remove the mitre and take off the garland,' which had been read as banning wedding garlands. Mar bar Rav Ashi answered that the ban is modeled on the High Priest, so it applies to men only, not to women.
why: The Gemara has just derived the ban on bridegrooms' garlands from a verse about the High Priest's mitre. This incident marks the limit of that ban: it covers grooms, not brides.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who questions Mar bar Rav Ashi.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who is braiding a wedding garland for his daughter.

terms.meaning: The turban worn by the High Priest in the Temple.

note: Rav Huna and Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef were sitting before Rabbi Yirmeya, who was dozing. Rav Huna argued that if a third party seizes a debtor's property for a creditor, he acquires it for him. Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef asked: even when that hurts other creditors? Rav Huna said yes. Just then Rabbi Yirmeya woke up and said to them: 'Children! This is what Rabbi Yoḥanan said: one who seizes property for a creditor where it hurts others does not acquire it.' He explained that the mishna's case is different, because anyone who says 'give' is like one who says 'acquire.'
why: The mishna rules that a master cannot take back a bill of freeing a slave once he hands it to an agent. Rav Huna tried to draw a rule about debt collection from that; Rabbi Yirmeya shows why the mishna does not prove it. Rav Ḥisda then links the question to an older dispute.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who draws a conclusion about seizing property for a creditor.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage who presses Rav Huna with a follow-up question.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: The senior Sage they sit before; he dozes, then wakes and corrects them.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage whose ruling Rabbi Yirmeya quotes.

terms.meaning: The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses. Here it is the ruling on bills freeing a slave.
To take legal ownership of something, here on behalf of someone else.

note: Some gardeners settled their accounts with each other, and one of them turned out to be holding five extra coins. The others told him, in front of the landowner, to give the money to the landowner, and the landowner made a formal act of acquisition with him. Later the gardener redid the sums himself and found he owed nothing. He came to Rav Naḥman, who said there was nothing he could do: a transfer made in the presence of all three parties is final, and the landowner had formally acquired the money besides. Rava objected that the gardener was not refusing to pay; he was saying the money was never owed. Rav Naḥman agreed: then it was an acquisition made in error, and any acquisition made in error is undone.
why: The Gemara has been discussing Rav's rule that a transfer made with all three parties present takes effect at once. Rav Naḥman applies that rule to this case, and Rava's objection shows where it stops: a transfer based on a mistake does not stand.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage the gardener comes to with his case.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who points out that the gardener is disputing the debt, not refusing to pay it.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Quoted by Rav Naḥman as the source of Rav's rule on transfers.

terms.meaning: A coin; five of them is the sum in dispute.
A formal legal act that makes a transfer of property or an obligation binding.

note: Rav Sheshet was owed money for cloaks he had given merchants to sell in the city of Meḥoza. He asked Rav Yosef bar Ḥama to bring him the money on his way back. Rav Yosef collected it, and the merchants asked to make a formal act of acquisition with him, which would make him responsible for the money on the road. He said yes, but in the end he slipped away without doing it. When he told Rav Sheshet, Rav Sheshet said he had done well. In one version, because he had not made himself the 'borrower who is a slave to the lender'. In another, because the merchants, as the borrowers, should bear the risk until the money arrives.
why: The Gemara is discussing who bears the risk when money is sent through a messenger, and whether the sender can take it back. This incident shows a messenger avoiding that risk, and Rav Sheshet approving.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A Sage owed money for cloaks sold in Meḥoza.

people.name: Rav Yosef bar Ḥama
people.about: The man Rav Sheshet sends to collect the money.

terms.meaning: A formal legal act that makes an obligation binding. Here it would have made Rav Yosef liable if the money were lost.

note: Rabbi Aḥai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya, had a silver vessel in the city of Neharde'a and asked Rabbi Dostai bar Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yosei bar Keifar to bring it to him. The people holding it handed it over, then demanded that the two accept formal responsibility for it. When they refused, the people demanded the vessel back. Rabbi Dostai agreed; Rabbi Yosei refused, and the people tormented him. When he appealed to Rabbi Dostai, Rabbi Dostai told them, 'Well done, hit him.' Back home Rabbi Yosei complained to Rabbi Aḥai, who asked Rabbi Dostai why he had done this. Rabbi Dostai described the men: huge, with frightening names, ready to tie up or kill anyone on command. Had they killed him, who would give his father Yannai another son like him? Rabbi Aḥai's reply is not given here.
why: The Gemara is discussing who bears the risk when an item is sent through messengers, and whether the senders may retract. Just before, Rav Sheshet's messenger avoided taking on that risk; here two messengers refuse it and the senders try to take the vessel back.

people.name: Rabbi Aḥai
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yoshiya; owner of the silver vessel.

people.name: Rabbi Dostai bar Rabbi Yannai
people.about: One of the two messengers; he gives in to the men and tells them to hit his colleague.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei bar Keifar
people.about: The other messenger, who refuses to return the vessel and is tormented for it.

people.name: Yannai
people.about: Rabbi Dostai's father, named in his defense.

terms.meaning: A formal legal act; here it would have made the messengers responsible for the vessel on the way.

flag: The STORY segments end with Rabbi Dostai's defense; Rabbi Aḥai's verdict ('you acted well') is in the next segment, outside the span.

note: The Sages told Rabbi Elazar of an incident: the mother of the sons of Rokhel, when ill, said, 'Give my brooch to my daughter.' The brooch was worth twelve hundred dinars. She died, and the Sages carried out her words. Rabbi Elazar answered with a curse: 'May their mother bury the sons of Rokhel.' The Gemara explains he meant that no proof can be drawn from that case: the sons were wicked, so the Sages let their sister have the jewel.
why: The Gemara is explaining a dispute about a dying person who sends money with the word 'deliver.' It ties that to a mishna in which Rabbi Elazar says a dying person's gift needs a formal act, and the Rabbis say words alone suffice. The Rabbis bring this incident as proof; Rabbi Elazar rejects it.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who holds that even a dying person's gift needs a formal act of acquisition.

people.name: The mother of the sons of Rokhel
people.about: An ill woman who left her brooch to her daughter by word alone, then died.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; twelve hundred of them made the brooch a very valuable piece.

note: Rabba bar bar Ḥana was ill, and Rav Yehuda and Rabba went to visit him. While there they asked him a legal question: must two people who bring a bill of divorce from overseas declare that it was written and signed in their presence? He said no, since if they testified that the divorce happened in their presence they would be believed anyway. Meanwhile a Persian priest came in and took the lamp away from them. Rabba said: 'Merciful One! Let us live either in Your shadow or in the shadow of the descendants of Esau,' meaning the Romans.
why: The discussion is about two messengers bringing a bill of divorce from abroad; Rabba bar bar Ḥana's answer bears on that. The lamp episode leads the Gemara to ask whether living under Rome is really better than under Persia.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: The sick Sage who is visited and answers the question.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: One of the two Sages who visit him.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The other visitor, who cries out after the lamp is taken.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.
A Zoroastrian priest. On a Persian festival, the translation explains, no one was allowed to keep a light burning outside their temple.

note: A man told ten men, 'Write a bill of divorce for my wife.' Two of them signed it that day, and the rest signed over the next ten days. He came to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi to ask whether it was valid. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said that Rabbi Shimon, who allowed a bill of divorce written by day and signed at night, is worthy of being relied on in a pressing situation, so the divorce stands.
why: The Gemara has just set out how Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish differ when a husband asks ten men to sign, including the case of two signing on the day and the rest later. This ruling is that very case, and the Gemara goes on to ask whose view it follows.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage who rules on the case.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: An earlier Sage whose lenient view Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi relies on.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage. It must be signed by witnesses.

note: A certain man let witnesses who could not sign their names trace them over a stencil on documents other than a bill of divorce. Rav Kahana had him flogged for it.
why: The Gemara has just said that letting witnesses trace their names is allowed only for bills of divorce, so that a woman is not left unable to remarry, and not for financial documents. This case shows that limit enforced.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: The Sage who orders the man flogged.

terms.meaning: Whipped; here a punishment given by the court for breaking a rule of the Sages.

note: A man threw what he said was a bill of divorce to his wife, among the barrels in her courtyard. Later all that was found there was a mezuza. Rav Naḥman ruled that a mezuza is rarely found among barrels, so it must be what the man threw, and not a bill of divorce.
why: The Gemara is asking when a document handed to a wife can be trusted as a bill of divorce, and when the husband can later say it was something else. Here the object itself is in doubt.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage who rules on the case.

terms.meaning: A small parchment scroll with verses from the Torah, fixed to a doorpost.
The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.

note: A man went into the synagogue, took a Torah scroll, gave it to his wife and said, 'This is your bill of divorce.' Rav Yosef asked why there should be any concern. If the worry is that he had written a bill of divorce on it in gall water that has since faded, gall water does not hold on parchment that was itself prepared with gall water.
why: The discussion just before deals with doubtful bills of divorce, and with gall water as a writing liquid. The Gemara goes on to say that Rav Yosef's real point is that rule: gall water does not stay on parchment prepared with gall water.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who rules that there is nothing to be concerned about.

terms.meaning: Water in which gallnuts were soaked, used as a writing liquid and to prepare parchment.
The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.

note: A bill of divorce turned up at Rav Huna's court. It named the place as 'Sheviri, the city on the Rakhis River,' and Rav Huna worried there might be two towns called Sheviri, so it might belong to a different couple. Rav Ḥisda told Rabba, then a student, to go and look into it, because Rav Huna would ask him about it that night. Rabba went, examined it, and found a mishna: all documents issued by a court are returned to their owner.
why: The Gemara is asking when a lost bill of divorce may be returned. It uses this incident to resolve an apparent contradiction between two rulings of Rabba: the worry about a second person with the same name counts only where two such people are known to exist.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage whose court the bill of divorce is brought to.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: A Sage who sends Rabba to look into the question.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: At this time a student; he finds the source that settles it.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses and quotes.

note: Rabba bar bar Ḥana lost a bill of divorce he was delivering, in the study hall. He said that if they asked for a distinguishing mark he had one, and if they relied on recognition by sight he could recognize it. They returned it to him. Afterward he said he did not know which was the reason: the distinguishing mark, meaning they held such marks count by Torah law, or his recognition, which is trusted only from a Torah scholar and not from an ordinary person.
why: The Gemara has just said that Rav Ashi was unsure whether returning a lost item by its distinguishing marks is Torah law or a rule of the Sages. Rabba bar bar Ḥana's case leaves the same question open.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: A Sage who loses a bill of divorce he was delivering and gets it back.

terms.meaning: A specific detail of a lost item, such as a hole next to a certain letter, that proves who owns it.
Knowing an item simply by sight, without naming a specific mark.
A rule from the Torah itself, as opposed to one the Sages added.

note: A man sent a bill of divorce to his wife with a messenger, who said he did not know her. The husband told him to give it to Abba bar Minyumi, who knew her, and he would deliver it. The messenger could not find Abba bar Minyumi, but he found Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa and Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa, with Rav Safra sitting among them. The three told him to hand his task over to them, and they would pass it to Abba bar Minyumi. Rav Safra objected that this messenger had never been given the power to carry out the divorce, so he could not pass it on. The three Sages were embarrassed.
why: The discussion just before is about when a messenger delivering a bill of divorce may appoint another in his place. Rava and Rav Ashi then argue over whether Rav Safra's objection was right.

people.name: Abba bar Minyumi
people.about: The man the husband trusted to recognize his wife and deliver the bill of divorce.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: One of three Sages who offer to take over the messenger's task.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa
people.about: One of the three Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa
people.about: One of the three Sages.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A Sage sitting with them who objects to their ruling.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.
A messenger appointed to act on someone's behalf, here to hand over a bill of divorce.

note: A man sent a bill of divorce to his wife with a messenger and told him not to deliver it for thirty days. Within the thirty days something beyond the messenger's control kept him from waiting. He came to Rava, who compared him to a messenger who falls ill and may appoint another, and told him to hand his task to the court, which would appoint a new messenger after thirty days. The Sages objected that he had no power to divorce yet; Rava answered that since he would have it after thirty days, he counts as having it. They objected again: perhaps the husband would make up with his wife in the meantime, and they cited a ruling to prove the concern. Rava was embarrassed. In the end it came out that the woman was only betrothed, and Rava said that worry does not apply to a betrothed woman.
why: Just before, Rav Safra ruled that a messenger never given the power to divorce cannot pass his task on. This case tests that rule on a messenger whose power only starts after thirty days. The Gemara then asks whether the court must appoint a new messenger in the first one's presence.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who rules on the case and defends his ruling.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Quoted by the Sages, citing his father Rav Huna in the name of Rav.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Father of Rabba bar Rav Huna, quoted in the name of Rav.

people.name: Rav
people.about: An earlier Sage whose ruling is cited against Rava.

terms.meaning: Formally engaged under Jewish law, which is already legally binding, though the couple do not yet live together.
Calmed and reconciled; the worry is that the husband made up with his wife and cancelled the divorce.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses and quotes.

note: A man left a bill of divorce with messengers and said: if I do not arrive within thirty days, let this be a divorce. He came back at the end of the thirtieth day, but the ferry was on the other side of the river and he could not cross. He called to the people across the river, 'See that I have arrived, see that I have arrived!' Shmuel said that does not count as arriving, so the divorce takes effect.
why: The discussion is about conditional divorces and circumstances outside a person's control. The next case, about a husband who could not appease his wife, is explained by whether such circumstances count in divorce law.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who rules that calling across the river is not arriving.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage. Here it was set to take effect only if he failed to return in time.

note: A man left a bill of divorce with messengers and said: if I do not make peace with my wife within thirty days, let this be a divorce. He went to appease her, but she would not be appeased. Rav Yosef said: did he give her a basket full of dinars and still she was not appeased? In this version, he had not truly met his own condition, so the divorce takes effect.
why: The Gemara gives a second version of Rav Yosef's ruling in which the divorce does not take effect, and explains the two as a dispute over whether circumstances beyond a person's control count in divorce law.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who rules on the case.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage. Here it was set to take effect only if he failed to make peace with her.
A silver coin.

note: Rav Huna and Rav Hisda were sitting together when Geneiva passed by. One of them said they should stand for him, since he was a man of Torah; the other objected: should we stand for a quarrelsome man? Meanwhile Geneiva came over and asked what they were studying. When they said winds, he passed on a teaching of Rav: four winds blow every day and the north wind blows with each of them, or the world could not survive an hour; the south wind is the harshest, and it would destroy the whole world if the angel Ben Netz did not hold it back.
why: The Gemara has been explaining the harsh east wind of Jonah and how the south wind silences the other winds; this encounter carries the theme of the winds further.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage sitting with Rav Hisda; one of the two debates whether to stand for Geneiva.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage sitting with Rav Huna when Geneiva passes.

people.name: Geneiva
people.about: A learned man whom one of the Sages calls quarrelsome; he joins them and teaches about the winds.

people.name: Ben Netz
people.about: An angel who, in the teaching Geneiva cites, holds back the south wind.

terms.meaning: A Torah scholar. Standing up when a scholar passes is a mark of respect, which is why the two Sages debate whether Geneiva deserves it.

note: Rava and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak were sitting when Rav Nahman bar Yaakov rode by in a gilded carriage under a green cloak. Rava went over to him; Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak stayed put, saying the riders were probably the Exilarch's people, whom Rava needed and he did not. When he saw who it was, he went over too. Rav Nahman bar Yaakov bared his arm and said the wind called Shadya was blowing. Rava cited Rav that a woman miscarries in that wind, Shmuel that even a pearl in the sea rots, and Rabbi Yohanan that even the seed in a woman's womb putrefies. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak pointed out that all three drew their teaching from a single verse in Hosea.
why: The Gemara is gathering teachings about winds, after Geneiva's account of the four winds. Right after this, Rava praises Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak as a man of Sura, where they are precise with verses.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who goes to greet Rav Nahman bar Yaakov at once and cites Rav on the Shadya wind.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who at first does not go over, thinking the riders are the Exilarch's people; he ties the three teachings to one verse.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yaakov
people.about: A Sage who rides by in a gilded carriage and remarks that the Shadya wind is blowing.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a powerful official with his own household and court.
The name of a hot, harmful wind; the Sages here describe the damage it causes.

note: Rabba bar bar Hana recalled that he was one of five elders sitting before Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha. A man came before Rabbi Yoshiya, who compelled him, against his will, to authorize a bill of divorce. Rabbi Yoshiya then told the elders: go and hide, and write the bill of divorce for her.
why: The Gemara wants to know which rulings follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and which follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in two disputes about cancelling a bill of divorce. It infers from the order to hide, rather than to scatter, that Rabbi Yoshiya followed one of them in each.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage who tells this as an eyewitness, one of the five elders present.

people.name: Rabbi Yoshiya from Usha
people.about: The Sage who compels the man to authorize the divorce and tells the elders to hide while writing it.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband must have written and delivered to his wife to end a marriage. A husband may try to cancel it before it reaches her.

note: Giddul bar Re'ilai sent a bill of divorce to his wife. The messenger found her sitting and weaving and told her: here is your bill of divorce. She said: at least go away for now and come back tomorrow. The messenger went back and told Giddul, who responded with the blessing: Blessed is He Who is good and does good. Abaye said that Giddul blessed God but the bill of divorce was still valid; Rava said that he blessed God and the bill of divorce was cancelled.
why: The Gemara has been discussing how a husband can cancel a bill of divorce he has sent. It explains that Abaye and Rava disagree over whether a husband merely showing that he no longer wants it delivered cancels it.

people.name: Giddul bar Re'ilai
people.about: A man who sends his wife a bill of divorce and then blesses God when it is not delivered.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who holds that the bill of divorce stays valid.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who holds that the bill of divorce is cancelled.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that ends a marriage once it is delivered to the wife; until then the husband may cancel it.

terms.term: Blessed is He Who is good and does good
terms.meaning: A blessing said on hearing good news. The translation explains that Giddul said it because he was glad the divorce had not been delivered.

note: Rav Sheshet compelled a certain man, against his will, to authorize a bill of divorce. The man then told the witnesses: this is what Rav Sheshet says to you, let the bill of divorce be cancelled. Rav Sheshet made him authorize another bill of divorce.
why: Rava cites this case to prove his view that a husband's showing he does not want the divorce cancels it. Abaye answers that the man had really cancelled it himself, and only blamed Rav Sheshet to avoid being flogged.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A Sage who forces a man to divorce his wife and then requires a second bill of divorce.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that ends a marriage. Witnesses write or sign it on the husband's instruction, and he can cancel it before it is delivered.

note: Rav Yehuda compelled the son-in-law of Rabbi Yirmeya Bira'a to authorize a bill of divorce, and the man cancelled it. Rav Yehuda compelled him again, and again he cancelled it. The third time Rav Yehuda compelled him against his will and told the witnesses: stuff gourd in your ears and write it for him. The man ran after the witnesses, but they could not hear him.
why: Abaye cites this case to prove that a husband merely showing he does not want the divorce does not cancel it: the witnesses could see him chasing them. Rava replies he might have been running to tell them to hurry.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who forces the man to divorce three times and has the witnesses block their ears.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya Bira'a
people.about: A Sage whose son-in-law is being compelled to divorce his wife.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that ends a marriage. A husband can cancel it by saying so before witnesses, which is why the witnesses here block their ears.

note: A man who was betrothed told witnesses: if I do not marry her within thirty days, let this be a bill of divorce. When the thirty days came, he told them: I tried, but could not. The text does not say what became of the divorce.
why: The Gemara asks what doubt there could be: circumstances beyond a man's control do not count for a bill of divorce, and if his words show he no longer wants it, that is the dispute of Abaye and Rava, where the ruling follows Abaye.

terms.meaning: In Talmudic law a couple was first betrothed, which already bound them as husband and wife, and only later married; ending a betrothal required a bill of divorce.
The document, called a get, that ends a marriage or a betrothal. A man could give one on a condition, so that it takes effect only if the condition is not met.

note: During years of famine a man left a gold dinar for safekeeping with a widow. She put it in a jar of flour, unknowingly baked it into a loaf of bread, and gave the loaf to a poor man. Some time later the owner came and asked for his dinar. She swore: may poison take hold of one of my children if I benefited at all from your dinar. Within a few days one of her children died. When the Sages heard, they said: if this happens to one who swears truthfully, how much more to one who swears falsely.
why: The mishna says courts stopped making widows swear an oath to collect their marriage payment. The Gemara asks whether this incident, showing how dangerous an oath is, was the reason, and then asks why it would apply only to widows.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: The Sage who reports this incident in the name of Rav; some say it was Rav Yehuda.

terms.meaning: A coin; a gold dinar was worth a good deal of money.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses and explains, line by line.

note: A widow came before Rav Huna to collect her marriage payment. He told her: what can I do for you, since Rav does not collect a marriage payment for a widow. She answered: isn't the only reason the worry that I already took some of it? As the Lord of Hosts lives, I have not benefited from my marriage contract at all. Rav Huna said: Rav agrees in the case of a woman who jumps in and swears of her own accord.
why: The Gemara has explained that Rav would not let widows collect, because the courts no longer had them swear and vows were taken lightly. Rav Huna's ruling carves out an exception to Rav's practice.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A judge who at first refuses the widow, citing Rav, then accepts her oath.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rav Huna's authority, who did not collect marriage payments for widows.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, a document promising a wife a sum of money if her husband dies or divorces her. A widow collects it from her late husband's estate, which now belongs to his heirs.
A woman who takes an oath on her own initiative, without the court asking her to.

note: A widow came before Rav Huna, who said he could not collect her marriage payment because Rav did not; she swore of her own accord that she had taken nothing, and Rav Huna ruled that Rav agrees in such a case. Another widow came before Rav Huna's son, Rabba bar Rav Huna, who told her that neither Rav nor his own father collected a marriage payment for a widow. She asked him at least to give her support. He said she had no right to that either, citing Shmuel: a widow who demands her marriage payment in court loses her support. She said: let his chair be overturned, he has treated me by the rulings of two different people. He overturned his chair and set it up again, and even so he was not spared from weakness.
why: The Gemara has explained Rav's refusal to let widows collect their marriage payment. Next, Rav Yehuda, Shmuel's student, tells a judge to find ways to let widows collect, against the practice of Rav's students.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A judge who follows Rav's practice but accepts a widow's oath taken of her own accord; father of Rabba bar Rav Huna.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Rav Huna's son, who refuses a widow both her marriage payment and her support, and is struck by her curse.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage whose ruling, that a widow who sues for her marriage payment loses her support, Rabba bar Rav Huna cites.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, a document promising a wife a sum of money if her husband dies or divorces her; a widow collects it from his estate.
Food and support a widow may draw from her late husband's estate as long as she has not claimed her marriage payment.

note: A certain teacher of young children was negligent with them. Rav Aha made him take a vow, with the community's consent, to stop teaching. Later Ravina reinstated him, because no one else could be found who was as careful in teaching as he was.
why: Ameimar ruled that a vow taken with the community's consent cannot be released. The Gemara limits this to vows about optional matters: for the sake of a commandment it can be released, as with this teacher.

people.name: Rav Aha
people.about: The Sage who has the negligent teacher vow, with the community's consent, to stop teaching.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The Sage who reinstates the teacher when no equally careful teacher can be found.

terms.term: vow on the consent of the public
terms.meaning: A vow whose terms depend on the community's agreement. Normally a Sage can release a person from a vow, but such a vow was held to be harder to undo.
A commandment or religious duty. Teaching children Torah counts as one.

note: A relative of Rabbi Asi held a loan document that included a guarantee on the borrower's property. He asked Rabbi Asi whether the Sabbatical Year cancels the debt, and was told it does not. He then went to Rabbi Yohanan, who said it does. Rabbi Asi came and asked Rabbi Yohanan himself, who again said it does. Rabbi Asi protested that Rabbi Yohanan himself had said it does not. Rabbi Yohanan replied: just because that is how we reason, should we act on it? When Rabbi Asi pointed to a teaching that supports him, Rabbi Yohanan answered that perhaps it follows Beit Shammai, who hold that a document waiting to be collected counts as already collected.
why: The Gemara has set out a dispute over whether the Sabbatical Year cancels loans backed by a property guarantee, with Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish saying it does not. This case shows Rabbi Yohanan refusing to rule by his own view in practice.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: A Sage who rules for his relative that the debt stands, then questions Rabbi Yohanan about his contrary ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Rabbi Asi's teacher, who rules that the debt is cancelled, even though he had reasoned otherwise.

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when by Torah law outstanding loans are cancelled and lenders may no longer demand repayment.
A clause in a loan document pledging the borrower's land as security, so the lender can collect from it.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the mishna, the main collection of their teachings.
The school of the early Sage Shammai, whose rulings are generally not followed in practice.

flag: The first STORY segment is a baraita stating the law, not part of the narrative; the story begins at the second STORY segment.

note: Abba bar Marta, also called Abba bar Minyumi, owed Rabba money. He brought it to him during the Sabbatical Year, and Rabba said: I cancel the debt. Abba took the money and left. Abaye found Rabba sad, and Rabba told him what had happened. Abaye went to Abba and asked whether he had answered: nevertheless, take it. Abba said no. Abaye told him that if he had, Rabba would have taken it, so he should bring it back now and say so. Abba did, and Rabba took the money. Rabba said: this young scholar had no sense to begin with.
why: The mishna says a lender paid in the Sabbatical Year must say he cancels the debt, but may accept if the borrower says: nevertheless. Rabba has just ruled the lender may hopefully wait for those words, and here he does.

people.name: Abba bar Marta
people.about: Also called Abba bar Minyumi; a young scholar who owes Rabba money and takes Rabba's words literally.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The lender, who formally cancels the debt and is saddened when the borrower takes him at his word.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who notices Rabba's sadness and coaches the borrower on what to say.

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when by Torah law outstanding loans are cancelled; a lender may accept repayment only if the borrower insists.
The formal words, I cancel the debt, that a lender must say when a borrower offers repayment in the Sabbatical Year.

note: Shmuel's maidservant was taken captive. Some people ransomed her as a maidservant and sent her back to him with a message: we follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and even if you follow the Rabbis, we ransomed her as a maidservant. The Gemara adds that they thought this happened before Shmuel had given up hope of getting her back, but in fact it was after. So Shmuel not only did not keep her as a slave; he did not even require her to receive a writ of freedom.
why: The mishna disputes whether a slave ransomed from captivity stays a slave, and the Gemara asks whether that depends on the owner having given up hope. Shmuel acts on his own view that a slave whose owner renounces him is free without a document.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Called Master Shmuel; his maidservant is captured and ransomed, and he treats her as a free woman.

terms.meaning: An owner's giving up hope of recovering something lost or taken. After that point the law can treat the item, or here the slave, as no longer his.
A writ of freedom: the document a master gives a slave to set him or her free.

terms.term: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis
terms.meaning: The two sides of the mishna's dispute over whether a slave ransomed from captivity remains a slave or goes free.

note: The maidservant of Rabbi Abba bar Zutra was taken captive, and a gentile ransomed her to be his wife. The Sages sent word to Rabbi Abba bar Zutra: if you want to do the right thing, send her a writ of freedom. The text does not say what he did.
why: The Gemara asks what a writ of freedom could achieve. It answers that the townspeople would then ransom her as a free Jewish woman, or that her captor would think less of her as a Jew's maidservant and let her be ransomed.

people.name: Rabbi Abba bar Zutra
people.about: A Sage whose maidservant is captured; the Sages advise him to free her.

terms.meaning: A writ of freedom: the document a master gives a slave to set him or her free.
A word the translation leaves untranslated; it describes the man as a gentile.

note: In Pumbedita there was a maidservant with whom men were committing forbidden sexual acts. Abaye said that, were it not for Shmuel's teaching that anyone who frees his slave violates a commandment, he would force her master to write her a writ of freedom. Ravina said that in a case like this one, even Shmuel's student Rav Yehuda agrees, because of the forbidden acts.
why: The Gemara is discussing when a slave may be freed. It goes on to challenge Abaye from a case where a court forced a master to free a half-slave woman, then distinguishes the two.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who would force the master to free her, if not for the teaching against freeing slaves.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who holds that freeing her is allowed in such a case.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who passes on Shmuel's teaching that freeing a slave violates a commandment.

terms.meaning: A commandment to do something. Shmuel reads the verse about keeping slaves forever as such a commandment, so freeing a slave breaks it.
A writ of freedom: the document a master gives a slave to set her free, after which she could marry a Jew.

note: In Pumbedita men were committing forbidden sexual acts with a certain maidservant. Abaye said that, were it not for Shmuel's teaching that freeing a slave violates a commandment, he would force her master to free her; Ravina said that in such a case even Rav Yehuda agrees she may be freed. The Gemara then recalls an incident told by Rabbi Yitzhak: a woman who was half maidservant and half free, whose master the court forced to set her fully free. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak explained that men had been treating her as if she belonged to no one.
why: The Gemara uses the half-free woman's case to ask whether Abaye really rejects freeing a slave to prevent sin. It answers that the cases differ: she could marry neither a slave nor a free man, while a full maidservant can be given to a slave who will guard her.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who would force the Pumbedita master to free his maidservant, if not for the teaching against freeing slaves.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who holds that freeing her is allowed because of the forbidden acts.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who explains why the court forced the half-free woman's master to free her.

terms.meaning: A woman owned by two masters, one of whom had freed his share of her, leaving her half free.
A commandment to do something. Shmuel reads the verse about keeping slaves forever as such a commandment.

flag: The span joins the Pumbedita maidservant case with the Gemara's objection that cites a separate incident (a half-free woman); the Pumbedita case alone is also its own story.

note: Rabbi Eliezer entered a synagogue and did not find the ten men needed for prayer. So he freed his slave, and the slave completed the ten.
why: Shmuel taught that freeing a slave violates a commandment. The Gemara raises Rabbi Eliezer's act as an objection and answers that freeing a slave for the sake of a commandment is different.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who frees his slave so that there will be ten men for prayer.

terms.meaning: The ten adult Jewish men needed for public prayer. A slave did not count toward it, but a freed slave did.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the mishna, the main collection of their teachings.

note: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak found Rava bar She'eilta standing at the door of a house of prayer and asked whether the law follows Rabbi Shimon. Rava bar She'eilta said: I say it does not, but the Sages who came from Mehoza report, in the name of Rav Nahman, that it does. The account goes on: when the speaker came to Sura, he asked Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin what had actually happened. He was told that a maidservant whose master lay dying came crying to him: how long will that woman stay enslaved? The master took his hat, threw it to her, and said: go acquire this, and acquire yourself. When they came before Rav Nahman, he said: he has done nothing.
why: Rabbi Shimon holds that a slave is freed only by a writ, not by payment, and the Sages disagree whether the law follows him. Next, the Gemara says Rav Nahman's ruling here did not rest on that view, but on the master having used his own hat for the transfer.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who asks whether the law follows Rabbi Shimon.

people.name: Rava bar She'eilta
people.about: A Sage, found at the door of a house of prayer, who answers and reports what others say.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin
people.about: A Sage in Sura who tells what actually happened in the case Rav Nahman ruled on.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage who rules that the dying master's act did not free the maidservant.

terms.meaning: Jewish law as it is actually practised; asking whether the halakha follows a Sage means asking whether his view is the binding one.
A way of transferring ownership by handing over an object; the master tried to give the maidservant ownership of herself by having her take his hat.

note: A town of slaves had been sold to gentiles. When their last gentile owners died, the slaves came before Ravina. He told them: go back to the children of your first owners and have them write you writs of freedom. The Sages objected that Ameimar had said a slave whose master renounced him and died has no remedy. Ravina answered that he followed Rav Dimi's report. They said Rav Dimi's report was mistaken. Ravina replied: mistaken only in that the master had not used words of freeing; had he used them, it would hold.
why: The Gemara has just recorded Ameimar and Rav Ashi debating whether a renounced slave can still be freed and whether Rav Dimi's report is mistaken. This case puts that debate into practice, and the Gemara rules like Ravina.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who tells the slaves to get writs of freedom from their first owners' children, and defends that ruling.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage whose ruling, that a renounced slave whose master has died has no remedy, the Sages raise against Ravina.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage whose report of Rabbi Yohanan's ruling Ravina relies on.

terms.meaning: A town or estate, here one whose people were slaves.
A writ of freedom: the document a master, or his heirs, gives a slave to set him free and let him live as a full Jew.
Words that actually declare a slave free, as opposed to a looser instruction about how heirs should treat the slave.

note: Two partners owned a slave together, and one of them freed his half. The other partner worried that the local rabbis would hear of it and make him lose the slave, so he transferred his half to his young son, whom the court could not force to free anyone. Rav Yosef, son of Rava, sent the case to Rav Pappa, who answered with a verse: as he has done, so shall it be done to him. Rav Pappa's plan: since a child is drawn to money, appoint a steward for the boy, have the slave jingle coins in front of him, and write a bill of emancipation in the boy's name.
why: The Gemara has just ruled, with Ravina, that a bill of manumission can still be written for slaves whose ownership seemed lost; this case shows the Sages finding a way to free a half-freed slave whose owner tried to block it.

people.name: Rav Yosef, son of Rava
people.about: Sent the case of the half-freed slave to Rav Pappa for a ruling.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Answered that the master's trick should be turned back on him, and laid out how to free the slave.

terms.meaning: A written document by which a master frees a slave. Also called a bill of manumission.
A guardian appointed to manage the property of a child or orphan who cannot legally manage it himself.

note: Rabbi Yitzhak reported an incident: a woman who was half slave and half free, whose master was forced to free her completely. The Gemara asks whether this follows Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka, who held that the blessing 'be fruitful and multiply' was spoken to both Adam and Eve, so a woman too must be able to have children. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak said no: the reason was that men were taking liberties with her, since she could not marry.
why: The Gemara has been debating what happens to the betrothal of a woman who is half slave and half free when she is freed; this incident shows a court forcing her full freedom, and the Gemara asks on what grounds.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: Reported the incident, through Rav Huna bar Ketina.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka
people.about: Sage who held that the command to have children applies to women as well as men.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: Explained that the master was forced to free her because men were taking liberties with her.

terms.meaning: A woman owned by two partners, one of whom freed his share. She is partly a slave and partly free, and so cannot legally marry either a free Jew or a slave.

note: A slave fled from his master outside the Land of Israel into the Land of Israel. His master followed him and came before Rabbi Ami. Rabbi Ami told the master: we will write you a promissory note for the slave's value, and you write him a bill of manumission. If you refuse, I will take him from you altogether, on the authority of Rabbi Ahai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya. The text does not say what the master did.
why: The Gemara has just discussed why a Jew who buys a slave abroad loses him; this case turns to a slave who flees into the Land of Israel, and the discussion after it explains the verse reading of Rabbi Ahai that Rabbi Ami relied on.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage before whom the master came; he pressed the master to free the slave.

people.name: Rabbi Ahai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya
people.about: Sage whose teaching Rabbi Ami cited as grounds for taking the slave from his master.

terms.meaning: A written document by which a master frees a slave.
A written promise to pay a debt, here for the slave's value, so the master would still be paid.

note: Rav Hisda's slave ran away to Bei Kutai, a place where Samaritans lived, and Rav Hisda sent asking them to return him. They answered with the verse 'You shall not deliver to his master a slave.' He replied with the verse on lost property: so you shall do with anything your brother has lost. They sent the first verse back again. Rav Hisda answered that it speaks of a slave who fled from outside the Land of Israel into it, as Rabbi Ahai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya, taught. The text does not say whether the slave was returned.
why: The Gemara has been collecting rival readings of the verse about not returning a runaway slave; right after, it asks why Rav Hisda chose Rabbi Ahai's reading and answers that this was how the Samaritans themselves understood the verse.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The master whose slave ran away; he argued by letter with the Samaritans for his return.

people.name: Rabbi Ahai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya
people.about: Sage whose reading of the verse Rav Hisda cited.

terms.meaning: A place where Samaritans lived. Samaritans were a group who accepted the Torah but not the teachings of the Sages.
The Land of Israel.

note: Abaye lost a donkey among the Samaritans of Bei Kutai and sent asking them to send it to him. They asked him to send a distinguishing mark first. He wrote that its belly was white. They sent back that if he were not Nahmani, they would not have sent it, since all donkeys have white bellies.
why: It comes right after Rav Hisda's exchange with the same Samaritans of Bei Kutai over his runaway slave, which turned on the verse about returning a brother's lost property.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who lost his donkey; the Samaritans call him Nahmani and trust him.

terms.meaning: A detail that identifies a lost item, which the owner gives to prove it is his before the finder returns it.
A place where Samaritans lived. Samaritans were a group who accepted the Torah but not the teachings of the Sages.

note: Rav Nahman's daughters would stir a boiling pot with their bare hands. Rav Ilish puzzled over the verse 'a woman among all these I have not found': what about Rav Nahman's daughters? His words brought on their captivity, and he was taken captive with them. In captivity a man who knew the language of birds told him a raven was calling 'Ilish, escape'; Ilish called the raven a liar. Then a dove said the same, and since Israel is compared to a dove, he took it as a sign of a miracle. He eavesdropped on the daughters and heard them say their captors were now their husbands and they did not want to be redeemed. He fled; he crossed the river by ferry, but the captors caught the other man and killed him. When the daughters came back, Ilish said they had stirred the pot by witchcraft.
why: The mishna has just ruled that one may not help captives escape, and the Gemara asked whether that holds when there is only one captive; this tale of an escape from captivity follows.

people.name: Rav Ilish
people.about: Questioned the daughters' righteousness, was taken captive with them, and escaped.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Father of the daughters who stirred the boiling pot and were taken captive.

people.name: the man who knew the language of birds
people.about: A fellow captive who interpreted the birds for Rav Ilish; he fled with him and was killed.

terms.meaning: The Jewish people as a whole, often pictured in the Sages' teachings as a dove.
A town in Babylonia, home of the daughters' husbands.

note: An Arab merchant woman brought a sack of phylacteries to Abaye. He asked whether she would give him each pair for a date. She became furious, took the phylacteries and threw them into the river. Abaye said: I should not have belittled them so much in front of her.
why: The Sages have just taught that one may pay a gentile somewhat more than their value for sacred objects, up to a small coin; Abaye's lowball offer shows what is lost by paying too little.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who offered a date for each pair of phylacteries and regretted it.

people.name: a certain Arab merchant woman
people.about: Brought the phylacteries to sell, and threw them into the river when insulted by the price.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: small leather boxes holding handwritten Torah verses, worn by Jewish men during prayer.

note: Some residents of Bei Mikhsi borrowed money from gentiles and could not pay it back, so the gentiles came and seized them as slaves. They came before Rav Huna to ask that they be redeemed. Rav Huna said: what can I do for you? We learned that one who sells himself to gentiles is not redeemed. Rabbi Abba objected that their teacher had taught that this applies only to one who sold himself three times. Rav Huna answered that these people do this habitually.
why: The mishna rules that a man who sells himself to gentiles is not redeemed, and Rav Asi limits it to one who did so three times; this case tests that limit against people who fell into debt again and again.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Sage before whom the seized debtors came; he declined to have them redeemed.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Objected to Rav Huna, citing the teaching that the rule applies only after a third sale.

terms.meaning: Bought back out of captivity or slavery, usually with community funds.
The early collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.

note: A man who had sold himself to gladiators came before Rabbi Ami and begged him to redeem him. Rabbi Ami said that if even a self-sold man's children are redeemed to keep them from ruin, all the more so here, where his life is at stake. The Sages told Rabbi Ami the man was an apostate: he had been seen eating meat from carcasses and torn animals. Rabbi Ami said perhaps he ate it out of appetite. They replied that at times he passed over permitted food to eat forbidden food. So Rabbi Ami told the man: Go, they do not allow me to redeem you.
why: The mishna rules that a man who sells himself to gentiles is not redeemed, though his children are; Rabbi Ami argues that the danger of death should outweigh that rule, until the man's open rejection of Jewish law decides it.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who wanted to redeem the man but was stopped by the Sages.

terms.meaning: Men who fought to the death for public entertainment; selling oneself to them put one's life at risk.
A Jew who has deliberately rejected Jewish law.
Meat forbidden to Jews: from animals that died without proper slaughter, or from animals with a fatal injury or defect.

note: Reish Lakish sold himself to gladiators and took with him a bag with a round stone inside. He knew that on a captive's last day his captors grant whatever he asks. On his last day they asked what he wanted. He said he wished to tie them up, seat them, and strike each one a blow and a half. He tied them and seated them, and each one he struck once died. Gritting his teeth, he said to each dead man: are you laughing at me? You still have half a blow coming. He killed them all. He came home and sat eating and drinking. When his daughter asked if he wanted something to lie on, he said: my belly is my pillow. When he died he left only a kav of saffron, and recited of himself the verse 'they leave their wealth to others'.
why: It follows the case of an apostate who sold himself to gladiators and could not be redeemed; here a great Sage who sold himself to gladiators frees himself.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Sage who sold himself to gladiators and killed them on his last day; known here for his great strength.

people.name: his daughter
people.about: Asked Reish Lakish whether he wanted something to lie on.

terms.meaning: Men who fought to the death for public entertainment.
A small measure of volume, a few pints.

note: A steward for orphans in Rabbi Meir's neighborhood was selling the orphans' land and buying slaves, and Rabbi Meir would not let him. In a dream Rabbi Meir was shown the words: I wish to destroy and you build? Even so, he paid no attention, saying that words in dreams neither raise nor lower anything.
why: The teaching just quoted forbids stewards to sell orphans' fields to buy slaves, since land is the safer asset; this case shows Rabbi Meir enforcing that rule even against a dream.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Sage who stopped the steward and ignored a dream that seemed to tell him otherwise.

terms.meaning: A guardian appointed to manage the property of orphans until they are old enough to manage it themselves.

note: Two men, incited by Satan, quarreled with each other every Friday at twilight. Rabbi Meir came to their place and held them back three Friday evenings in a row until he made peace between them. Then he heard Satan say: Woe, Rabbi Meir has driven that man out of his house.
why: The Gemara says it tells this one because it has just told another story about Rabbi Meir and a steward for orphans.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Sage who made peace between the two quarreling men.

people.name: Satan
people.about: Incited the quarrel, and lamented when Rabbi Meir ended it.

terms.meaning: The hour just before the Sabbath begins, when tension is high as preparations must be finished.

note: A steward for orphans in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's neighborhood was selling the orphans' land and buying oxen, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said nothing to him at all.
why: The rule just taught forbids selling orphans' land to buy slaves; the Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi agreed with Rabbi Yosei, who called his ox 'my field', so oxen count as land.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Sage who saw the steward trade land for oxen and did not object.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Sage who said he never called his wife 'my wife' but 'my home', nor his ox 'my ox' but 'my field'.

terms.meaning: A guardian appointed to manage the property of orphans until they are old enough to manage it themselves.

note: Some orphans lived with an old woman, and they owned an ox, which she took and sold for them. Their relatives came before Rav Nahman asking what right she had to sell. He said the mishna speaks of orphans who live with a householder, so she counts as their steward. They objected that the ox had since gone up in value; he said it rose while in the buyer's hands. They objected that the orphans had not yet been paid. Rav Nahman said that in that case Shmuel's rule applies: orphans' property is like consecrated property and changes hands only when money is paid. The text does not say how the sale ended.
why: It follows a run of cases about stewards of orphans' property; this one asks who may act as steward without being appointed, and leads into Shmuel's rule on when an orphans' sale becomes final.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage before whom the orphans' relatives challenged the sale.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage whose rule on orphans' property Rav Nahman cited.

people.name: Rav Hanilai bar Idi
people.about: Passed on Shmuel's rule about orphans' property.

terms.meaning: Property given to the Temple. By law it changes hands only when money is paid, not by the buyer taking hold of it as with ordinary goods.
A guardian who manages orphans' property for them.

note: Buyers took possession of the wine of Rabbana Ukva, an orphan, at four dinars a barrel. Before they paid, its price rose to six. The parties came before Rav Nahman, who said this case falls under Shmuel's rule: orphans' property is like consecrated property and changes hands only when money is paid.
why: It applies the rule Rav Nahman cited in the case just before; the Gemara then works out when that rule helps orphans, and Rav Sheisha objects that it could harm them.

people.name: Rabbana Ukva
people.about: An orphan whose wine rose in price before the buyers had paid.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage who ruled on the sale of the wine.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage whose rule on orphans' property Rav Nahman cited.

terms.meaning: A legal act of acquisition: taking physical hold of goods. For ordinary goods this finalizes a purchase.
Property given to the Temple, which changes hands only when money is paid.

note: Amram the dyer was a steward for orphans. The orphans' relatives came to Rav Nahman and said he dressed himself in fine clothes from the orphans' property. Rav Nahman said: perhaps so that his words will be listened to. They said he ate and drank from their property though he was not known to be rich. Rav Nahman said: say he found something valuable. They said he was causing them losses. Rav Nahman said: bring me witnesses that he causes losses and I will remove him, citing Rav Huna in Rav's name that a steward who causes losses is removed.
why: The Gemara is working through the duties of a steward for orphans; this case sets the rule, disputed by the school of Rabbi Sheila, that a steward who causes loss is removed, and the Gemara rules that he is.

people.name: Amram the dyer
people.about: Steward for orphans, accused by their relatives of living off their property.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage who heard the complaints and asked for witnesses before removing the steward.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Reported in Rav's name that a steward who causes losses is removed.

terms.meaning: A guardian appointed to manage the property of orphans until they are old enough to manage it themselves.
The binding ruling in Jewish law.

note: One man insulted another, calling him a convert, son of a convert. The second man shot back: at least I don't eat produce of the Sabbatical Year the way you do.
why: The Gemara is explaining why Rabbi Yehuda imposed no penalty for unknowingly breaking the Sabbatical Year rules: in his place it was treated as very serious, and this exchange, where eating its produce is the worse insult, is the proof.

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when fields in the Land of Israel must lie fallow and their produce may not be traded or treated as ordinary.
Someone who became Jewish rather than being born Jewish; here the word is used as an insult.

note: A man told another: the ritually pure food I prepared with you on such and such a day became impure. The owner came before Rabbi Ami, who said that in principle the man is not believed. Rabbi Asi said to him: My teacher, do you say this? Rabbi Yohanan said in Rabbi Yosei's name: What can I do, when the Torah believed him? The text does not say how Rabbi Ami responded.
why: A teaching just quoted says a helper is believed that food became impure while he is still working on it, but not about a past day; Rabbi Asi's report challenges that, and the Gemara next asks where the Torah believes such a person.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who ruled that the man is not believed about the past.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: Challenged Rabbi Ami, citing Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Reported Rabbi Yosei's saying that the Torah believes such a person.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Sage who said, What can I do, when the Torah believed him?

terms.meaning: Food kept free of ritual impurity, a religious status that contact with certain things can transfer. Impure food could not be eaten by those keeping these rules.

note: A scribe came before Rabbi Ami and said that in the Torah scroll he wrote for a client, he had not written God's names with the proper intention. Rabbi Ami asked who had the scroll; the buyer did. Rabbi Ami said: you are believed to lose your wage, but not to make the Torah scroll unfit. Rabbi Yirmeya asked: granted he loses his wage for the names, does he lose his wage for the whole scroll? Rabbi Ami said yes, since a Torah scroll whose names of God were not written with proper intention is worth nothing.
why: The Gemara is asking when a person is believed about past work he did for others; next it asks why the scribe was not told to go over the names again, and whose opinion that follows.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who ruled that the scribe's confession costs him his wage but does not disqualify the scroll.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Asked whether the scribe loses his pay for the whole scroll.

terms.meaning: A scribe must consciously intend each name of God as holy as he writes it; without that, the name, and so the scroll, is invalid.

note: A scribe came before Rabbi Abbahu and said that he had not prepared the parchment of a Torah scroll he wrote for a client with the proper intention. Rabbi Abbahu asked who had the scroll; the buyer did. Rabbi Abbahu said: since you are believed to lose your wage, you are believed to make the Torah scroll unfit.
why: It contrasts with Rabbi Ami's ruling just before; the Gemara explains that Rabbi Ami's scribe may have lied, thinking he would lose only part of his pay, while this scribe knew he was giving up his entire wage, so he is believed.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Sage who ruled that the scribe's confession disqualifies the scroll.

terms.meaning: Animal skin prepared for writing. For a Torah scroll it must be processed with the intention that it is for that holy use.

note: Rava raises a problem: a teaching says that a thief who consecrates a stolen animal and then slaughters it outside the Temple is punishable by karet. But if the thief never truly owned the animal, how could his consecration count? Rav Sheizevi answered that it is karet by rabbinic law, and the listeners laughed at him, since there is no such thing. Rava told them: A great man has spoken, do not laugh at him. He explained that Rav Sheizevi meant a karet that comes about through the Sages' words: the Sages placed the animal in the thief's possession so that he would become liable for it.
why: The Gemara is weighing Ulla's and Rav Yehuda's views on whether the Sages made a stolen offering valid or invalid; Rava's objection tests whether an owner's despair alone lets a thief acquire what he stole.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who raises the objection and then defends Rav Sheizevi when others laugh at him.

people.name: Rav Sheizevi
people.about: A Sage whose answer, karet by rabbinic law, is laughed at; Rava calls him a great man.

terms.meaning: A severe punishment in the Torah, usually understood as being cut off from one's people by God, given for certain grave sins such as sacrificing an offering outside the Temple.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of rabbinic law.
Dedicated to the Temple as an offering, so that it becomes sacred property.

note: Rabbi Yohanan says that Jerusalem was destroyed on account of Kamtza and bar Kamtza. A man held a feast and told his servant to bring his friend Kamtza, but the servant brought his enemy bar Kamtza. The host ordered him out. Bar Kamtza begged to stay, offering to pay for what he ate, then for half the feast, then for all of it, but the host refused each time and threw him out by the hand. Since the Sages present had not protested, bar Kamtza went to the emperor and said the Jews had rebelled, and proved it by having the emperor send an offering, which he blemished on the way. The Sages thought to sacrifice it anyway, or to kill bar Kamtza, but Rabbi Zekharya ben Avkolas objected to each plan.
why: The mishna's law of Sicarii is tied to the war against Rome, and the Gemara now turns to how that war and the destruction of the Temple began, opening with a verse about one who hardens his heart.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who links the destruction of Jerusalem to Kamtza and bar Kamtza.

people.name: Kamtza
people.about: The host's friend, whom he meant to invite.

people.name: bar Kamtza
people.about: The host's enemy, brought by mistake, humiliated and thrown out, who then informs against the Jews to the emperor.

people.name: Rabbi Zekharya ben Avkolas
people.about: A Sage who objects both to sacrificing the blemished animal and to killing bar Kamtza.

terms.meaning: A physical defect that makes an animal unfit to be offered on the altar under Jewish law.
A place named in Rabbi Yohanan's list of places destroyed through small causes; here, on account of a rooster and a hen.
A city whose destruction Rabbi Yohanan blames on a broken carriage shaft.

note: The Romans sent Nero Caesar against the Jews. When he came to Jerusalem he shot arrows to the east, the west and all four directions, and every one fell in Jerusalem. He then asked a child to recite the verse he had learned, and the child answered: And I will lay My vengeance upon Edom by the hand of My people Israel. Nero concluded that God wished to destroy His Temple and then wipe His hands on him, the one who did it. He fled and became a convert, and Rabbi Meir descended from him.
why: It continues the Gemara's account of the war that destroyed the Second Temple, which began with bar Kamtza's slander; the Roman response comes in stages, and Nero is the first general sent.

people.name: Nero Caesar
people.about: The Roman sent against the Jews, who tests his fate, flees and converts.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage the text says descended from Nero.

terms.meaning: The nation descended from Esau; the Sages associated Rome with Edom, which is why Nero heard the verse as being about him.

note: The Romans sent Vespasian, who laid siege to Jerusalem for three years. Three wealthy men lived in the city, Nakdimon ben Guryon, ben Kalba Savua and ben Tzitzit HaKesat, and the Gemara explains each name. One offered to feed the people with wheat and barley, one with wine, salt and oil, and one with wood; together they had enough to sustain the city for twenty-one years. The Sages wanted to go out and make peace with the Romans, but the zealots in the city would not allow it and wanted to fight. When the Sages said a battle would not succeed, the zealots burned the storehouses of wheat and barley, and famine followed.
why: It continues the Gemara's account of the war that ended in the destruction of the Temple, moving from Nero to Vespasian's siege.

people.name: Vespasian Caesar
people.about: The Roman sent to besiege Jerusalem.

people.name: Nakdimon ben Guryon
people.about: One of three wealthy men in Jerusalem, named for the sun shining on his behalf.

people.name: ben Kalba Savua
people.about: One of three wealthy men; anyone who entered his house hungry as a dog left satisfied.

people.name: ben Tzitzit HaKesat
people.about: One of three wealthy men, named for his fringes dragging on blankets, or his seat among the nobles of Rome.

people.name: Rav Hisda
