people.about: A Sage cited to show why wood was the most valued gift.

terms.meaning: Militant rebels inside besieged Jerusalem who wanted to fight Rome and overruled the Sages.

note: During the famine, Marta bat Baitos, one of the wealthy women of Jerusalem, sent her agent for fine flour. Each time he went, it was already sold, and so with ordinary flour, coarse flour and barley flour. Though she had just taken off her shoes, she went out herself to look for food; dung stuck to her foot, and she died. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai read a verse about her, about the tender woman who would not set her foot on the ground. Others say she ate one of Rabbi Tzadok's figs, sucked dry during his forty years of fasting, and died of disgust. As she was dying she threw all her gold and silver into the marketplace, saying: Why do I need this?
why: The zealots have just burned the city's food stores and brought famine; this story shows what that famine did, even to the richest of Jerusalem.

people.name: Marta bat Baitos
people.about: One of the wealthy women of Jerusalem during the siege.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: A Sage who applies a verse from the Torah's curses to her.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: A Sage who fasted forty years so Jerusalem would not be destroyed, and lived on the juice of figs.

note: Abba Sikkara, head of the zealots of Jerusalem, was the son of Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's sister. Rabban Yohanan called him in secret and asked how long they would go on killing everyone by starvation. Abba Sikkara said if he spoke up the zealots would kill him, so Rabban Yohanan asked for a way out of the city. Abba Sikkara told him to pretend to be sick, lay something rotting beside him so people would think he had died, and be carried out by his students alone. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua carried him; when the guards wanted to pierce or push the body, Abba Sikkara stopped them, and the gate was opened. Reaching the Roman camp, Rabban Yohanan greeted Vespasian as king; Vespasian said he deserved death twice over. The text here stops as Rabban Yohanan begins his answer.
why: It follows the famine the zealots caused in besieged Jerusalem; Rabban Yohanan sees no way to change their course inside the city and hopes that leaving it may bring some small salvation.

people.name: Abba Sikkara
people.about: Leader of the zealots of Jerusalem and nephew of Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: A Sage who escapes the besieged city in a coffin to meet the Roman commander.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: One of the students who carries Rabban Yohanan out.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: One of the students who carries Rabban Yohanan out.

people.name: Vespasian
people.about: The Roman commander besieging Jerusalem, to whom Rabban Yohanan comes.

terms.meaning: Militant rebels inside besieged Jerusalem who would not let anyone make peace with Rome.

flag: The STORY ends mid-sentence: Rabban Yohanan's reply to Vespasian (you are indeed a king) and the rest of the encounter continue in the AFTER segments.

note: Vespasian sent Titus, whom the Gemara calls the wicked one who blasphemed God. Titus took a prostitute into the Holy of Holies, spread out a Torah scroll and sinned with her on it, then cut the Temple curtain with his sword; by a miracle blood spurted out, and he thought he had killed God. He wrapped the Temple vessels in the curtain and shipped them to Rome to be praised. At sea a wave threatened to drown him, and he mocked God as powerful only in water. A Divine Voice told him to fight a lowly creature, the gnat, on dry land. A gnat entered his nose and picked at his brain for seven years; a blacksmith's hammering quieted it for thirty days only. When he died they found it grown to the size of a bird. Dying, he ordered his body burned and the ashes scattered so God could not judge him.
why: It continues the Gemara's account of the destruction: after Vespasian leaves for Rome, Titus completes the conquest, and the Gemara tells how he desecrated the Temple and how he was punished.

people.name: Titus
people.about: The Roman sent by Vespasian, who desecrates the Temple and is tormented by a gnat until his death.

people.name: Abba Hanan
people.about: A Sage who reads a verse as praising God's restraint in staying silent before Titus's blasphemy.

people.name: Rabbi Pinehas ben Arova
people.about: A Sage who says he was among the noblemen of Rome when Titus died and saw the gnat found in his head.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who reports a tradition that the gnat had a copper mouth and iron claws.

terms.meaning: The innermost chamber of the Temple, which only the High Priest entered, once a year.
A voice from heaven, the way the Talmud describes God speaking to people after the age of prophecy.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

note: Onkelos bar Kalonikos, the son of Titus's sister, wanted to convert. He raised Titus from the dead by sorcery and asked who is most important in that world. Titus said: the Jewish people. Should I join them? Titus answered that their commandments are many and he would not be able to keep them; better to fight them, since anyone who distresses Israel becomes a chief. Onkelos asked about Titus's own punishment. Titus answered that it is what he decreed against himself: every day his ashes are gathered, he is judged, burned and scattered over the seven seas.
why: It follows directly on Titus's death, when he ordered his ashes scattered so that God could not judge him; this tells what his punishment turned out to be.

people.name: Onkelos bar Kalonikos
people.about: The son of Titus's sister, who wants to convert and raises the dead to ask their advice.

people.name: Titus
people.about: Onkelos's uncle, the Roman who destroyed the Temple, raised from the dead here.

terms.meaning: Raising or summoning the dead to speak with them, a practice the Torah forbids.

flag: The STORY covers only the first of three linked consultations; Onkelos's sessions with Balaam and Jesus continue in the AFTER segments as part of the same story.

note: Rabbi Elazar says that God took bar Kamtza's side over his humiliation and destroyed His Temple. The Gemara then explains how the King's Mountain was destroyed on account of a rooster and a hen. It was the custom there to carry a rooster and a hen before a bride and groom, as if to say: be fruitful and multiply like chickens. Roman soldiers once took the birds and the people beat them; told the Jews had rebelled, the emperor came against them. Bar Deroma, who could leap a mil, killed many Romans, until the emperor set his crown on the ground and prayed to God. Bar Deroma then spoke a verse as a complaint against God; in an outhouse a snake eviscerated him and he died. The emperor left, but when the people celebrated with many lamps, he said they were rejoicing over him and came back.
why: Earlier Rabbi Yohanan named three places destroyed through small causes; having told of Jerusalem and Kamtza, the Gemara now gives the account of the second, the King's Mountain.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who teaches how great the power of shame is, as shown by bar Kamtza.

people.name: bar Kamtza
people.about: The man humiliated at the feast, whom God is said to have assisted.

people.name: bar Deroma
people.about: A man of the King's Mountain who could leap a mil and killed many Romans.

people.name: David
people.about: The psalmist, whose verse bar Deroma repeated; the Gemara says David said it as a question.

terms.meaning: A measure of distance, roughly a kilometer.
A region of the Land of Israel that the Gemara says was densely populated before the war.

flag: Segment 4 (Rabbi Elazar on bar Kamtza) concludes the previous Kamtza story and is not part of the King's Mountain story that follows; the massacre that ends the King's Mountain story is in the AFTER segment.

note: Three Sages were sitting together and asked whether anyone had heard anything about the town of Kefar Sekhanya. One of them told of a betrothed man and woman who were taken captive, and their captors married them to each other. She said to him: Please do not touch me, as I have no marriage contract from you. He did not touch her until the day he died. When he died, she told the Sages to eulogize him as a man who conquered his passion more than Joseph: Joseph was tested for a short time, not in one bed, and not with his own wife, while this man was tested every day, in one bed, with his own wife.
why: The Gemara is speaking of the towns of the King's Mountain region and how they were destroyed; three Sages share what they heard of one such town, and this is the first account.

people.name: Joseph
people.about: The biblical figure who resisted Potiphar's wife; the woman compares her husband to him.

terms.meaning: In Jewish law, the first stage of marriage: the couple are legally bound but do not yet live together.
The ketubba, the document that secures a wife's financial rights; the woman holds that they may not live together without one.

note: Another Sage told of a man who wanted to divorce his wife but did not want to pay her large marriage contract. He invited his friends, got them drunk and laid them in one bed with his wife, put egg white between them, brought witnesses and went to court claiming adultery. Bava ben Buta, an elder among the disciples of Shammai the Elder, was there and said he had a tradition: egg white hardens under fire, while semen is absorbed. They tested it and found he was right. They brought the husband to court, gave him lashes, and made him pay her marriage contract.
why: Three Sages are telling what they know of the town of Kefar Sekhanya in the King's Mountain region; after the discussion Abaye asks why such righteous people were destroyed.

people.name: Bava ben Buta
people.about: An elder among the disciples of Shammai the Elder, who exposes the husband's trick.

people.name: Shammai the Elder
people.about: The teacher from whom Bava ben Buta received the tradition about egg white.

terms.meaning: The ketubba, which promises a wife a sum of money on divorce; a wife proven to have committed adultery could lose it.
A court-imposed punishment of flogging.

note: Four hundred boys and girls were taken captive to be used for prostitution. Sensing what was intended for them, they asked whether they would reach the World-to-Come if they drowned themselves in the sea. The oldest among them expounded a verse, I will bring them back from the depths of the sea, as speaking of those who drown in the sea. When the girls heard this, they all leapt into the sea. The boys reasoned that if the girls did so, they all the more so should, and they too leapt into the sea. The verse For Your sake we are killed all the day long is said of them.
why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of the calamities that befell Israel in the destruction; this one ends with a verse, and the next account applies the same verse to another case of martyrdom.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, in which the righteous are rewarded.
An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one: if it holds for them, it holds all the more for us.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

note: A woman's seven sons were brought one by one before the emperor and told to worship an idol. Each refused, citing a different verse of the Torah, and each was taken out and killed. The emperor pitied the youngest and offered to throw down his seal so the boy could pick it up and seem to accept his authority. The boy answered: Woe to you, Caesar; if this is for your honor, how much more for the honor of God. As he was taken out to be killed, his mother asked to kiss him and told him: Go and tell your father Abraham, you bound one altar, but I bound seven. She went up to the roof, fell and died, and a Divine Voice proclaimed: A joyful mother of children.
why: The children who drowned themselves were tied to the verse For Your sake we are killed all the day long; Rav Yehuda says the verse refers to this woman and her seven sons.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who applies the verse to this woman and her sons.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The ruler who orders each son to worship an idol and has them killed.

people.name: Abraham
people.about: The patriarch who bound his son on the altar; the mother sends him a message through her son.

terms.meaning: A voice from heaven, the way the Talmud describes God speaking after the age of prophecy.
The emperor's signet; picking it up would look like bowing to his authority.

note: At first the noblemen of Rome kept an engraved image near their beds when they had intercourse, hoping for beautiful children. After the war, they tied Jewish children to the foot of their beds instead. Two children treated this way spoke to each other. One asked where this affliction is written in the Torah; the other cited: every sickness and every plague which is not written in the book of this Torah. The first asked how far he was from that verse in his studies, and was told a column and a half. He said: Had I got that far, I would not have needed you.
why: The Gemara has just read the precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, as describing children so beautiful they put fine gold to shame; this shows what their beauty brought on them.

terms.meaning: A column of a Torah scroll; the child measures his progress in study by how far he had read.

note: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that there were four hundred synagogues in the city of Beitar, each with four hundred schoolteachers, each teaching four hundred children. When the enemy entered, the schoolchildren stabbed them with their pens. When the enemy prevailed and caught them, they wrapped the children in their scrolls and set them on fire.
why: It explains a verse from Lamentations, My eye affects my soul because of all the daughters of my city, as part of the Gemara's run of accounts of what happened to Jewish children in the destruction.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage in whose name the account and its verse are given.

terms.meaning: A city whose fall to Rome the Gemara has been describing.

note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya went to Rome and was told of a child in prison with beautiful eyes and curly hair. He stood at the prison door and recited: Who gave Jacob for a spoil, and Israel to the robbers? The child answered with the rest of the verse: Did not the Lord, against Whom we have sinned? Rabbi Yehoshua said he was certain the child would issue rulings in Israel, and swore by the Temple service not to move until he ransomed him for any price. He paid a great sum, and within a few days the child was issuing rulings. He was Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha.
why: The Gemara is gathering accounts of what became of Jewish children in the destruction; this one is introduced as another teaching about their fate.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage who goes to Rome and ransoms a captive child.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
people.about: The captive child, who soon becomes a Sage issuing rulings.

terms.meaning: Paying captors to free a captive, a duty the Sages held to be very important.
A form of oath, swearing by the worship in the Temple.

note: The son and daughter of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha were taken captive and sold to two different masters. The masters met; one boasted of a male slave whose beauty had no equal in the world, the other of a female slave just as beautiful. They decided to marry the two and divide the children, and shut them in a room. The son sat in one corner and the daughter in the other. He said: I am a priest, descended from High Priests; shall I marry a slave woman? She said the same of a slave man. They wept all night. At dawn they recognized each other, fell on each other weeping until their souls departed. Jeremiah's lament, For these things I weep, is said of them.
why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha himself was ransomed as a child from captivity in Rome; this follows with what happened to his own son and daughter.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
people.about: A High Priest whose son and daughter were taken captive.

people.name: Jeremiah
people.about: The prophet whose lament is applied to the brother and sister.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple; the children's pride in their priestly line is why each refuses to marry a slave.

note: Reish Lakish tells of a woman named Tzafenat bat Peniel, called so because everyone gazed at her beauty and because she was the daughter of a High Priest who served in the innermost sanctum. Her captor abused her all night, then dressed her in seven garments and took her out to sell her. An especially ugly man asked to see her beauty; the seller told him to buy her or not, since there was no beauty like hers. When he insisted, the seller removed six garments; she tore the seventh herself, rolled in ashes, and said to God: Master of the Universe, even if You have shown no pity to us, why have You not shown pity to the sanctity of Your mighty name?
why: It is one in a run of accounts of the children of priestly families taken captive in the destruction, following the story of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha's son and daughter.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: The Sage who tells this account.

people.name: Tzafenat bat Peniel
people.about: A beautiful woman, daughter of a High Priest, taken captive and put up for sale.

terms.meaning: The Holy of Holies, the inner chamber of the Temple entered only by the High Priest.

note: A carpenter's apprentice set his eyes on his master's wife. When the master needed a loan, the apprentice told him to send his wife to him. He kept her for three days, then came back first and claimed he had sent her home at once but heard she had been abused on the road. He advised his master to divorce her, and when the master said her marriage contract was too large, lent him the money to pay it. The master divorced her and the apprentice married her. When the loan fell due and the master could not pay, the apprentice made him work off the debt by serving drinks to the couple as they ate, and his tears fell into their cups. The Gemara says the sentence on the Jewish people was sealed at that hour; some say it was for their adultery.
why: Rav Yehuda tells it to explain the verse So they oppress a man and his house, as a last account of the sins and sorrows of the destruction before the Gemara returns to the mishna's law of Sicarii.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who tells the account in Rav's name to explain a verse from Micah.

terms.meaning: The ketubba, which promises a wife a sum of money if her husband divorces her.
A euphemism for the adultery of the apprentice and the woman while she was still married to her first husband.

note: Giddel bar Re'ilai took over land in a valley in return for paying its land tax, and paid three years in advance. After the first year the original owners came back and said: you have eaten the produce for the year you paid; now we will pay and we will eat. The case came before Rav Pappa, who thought to give Giddel a document letting him claim the land from the valley's residents. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, objected that this would treat the case like that of a Sicarius. Instead he ruled that Giddel had put his money on the horn of a deer: he had risked it himself and could not claim it back.
why: Rav Yosef has just said the law of unjust seizure is not applied in Babylonia, since owners there can complain to the government; this case tests how far that reaches.

people.name: Giddel bar Re'ilai
people.about: A man who paid three years' land tax in advance in return for using the land.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The judge before whom the case was brought.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who objects to Rav Pappa's plan and rules against Giddel.

terms.meaning: In this discussion, someone who seized land by violence or threats; the Sages set special rules for buying land from such a person.
A tax owed by the residents of the valley on their land, paid jointly.

terms.term: on the horn of a deer
terms.meaning: A saying for money put somewhere it can run off: Giddel risked it by paying in advance.

note: Rav Shimi bar Ashi asked Abaye to set a time to study with him. Abaye said his daytime study was taken and at night he had to irrigate his fields, so Rav Shimi offered to do the irrigating by day so they could study at night, and Abaye agreed. Rav Shimi told the owners of the upper fields that the lower fields drink first, and told the lower owners that the upper fields drink first; while they argued, he dammed the river and watered Abaye's fields. Abaye told him he had acted on two opposing opinions at once, and would not taste that year's produce.
why: The Gemara has just said that since the law follows neither Rav (lower fields first) nor Shmuel (upper fields first), whoever is stronger prevails. Rav Shimi plays the two opinions against each other, and Abaye rejects water gained that way.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Ashi
people.about: A student who wants to study with Abaye and offers to irrigate his fields in exchange.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The teacher whose fields are watered; he refuses to eat the crop that came from the trick.

terms.meaning: Two Sages who disagreed over which fields along a river get the water first: in this story, Rav's view is that the lower fields drink first and Shmuel's that the upper fields do.

note: The people of a place called Bei Harmakh dug a channel at the head of the Shanvata River to run its water around their fields, then let it back into the river further down. The owners of the upstream fields complained to Abaye that this was damaging their river. Abaye told them to dig a little deeper alongside, but they said that would dry out their pits. Abaye then told the people of Bei Harmakh to take themselves away from there.
why: It follows another story about Abaye and disputes over river water for irrigation, part of the Gemara's discussion of who has first rights to shared water.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage the upstream field owners bring their complaint to.

note: Rav Kahana was walking to Huzal when he saw a man throwing sticks at a palm tree to knock down dates. Rav Kahana gathered some of the fallen dates and ate them. The man told him that he had thrown them down with his own hand, so they were his. Rav Kahana answered that he must be from the town of Rabbi Yoshiya, and applied to Rabbi Yoshiya the verse: "And a righteous man is the foundation of the world."
why: The mishna says that taking olives that fall from a tree a poor man is gleaning is robbery only by the Sages' rule for the sake of peace, but a Sage taught that once they were in his hand it is full robbery. The man's claim matches that teaching, and Rav Kahana credits his town's learning.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who eats dates a stranger knocked down, and accepts the man's claim that they were his.

people.name: Rabbi Yoshiya
people.about: A great Sage of Huzal; Rav Kahana credits him for the townsman's knowledge of the law.

terms.meaning: A town; the translation describes it as the place of Rabbi Yoshiya and a center of Torah study.

note: Rav Huna and Rav Hisda were sitting when the Sage Geneiva passed by. One said they should stand for him because he was learned in Torah; the other asked whether they should stand for an argumentative man. Geneiva came over and greeted them twice: "Peace be upon you, kings." They asked how he knew Sages are called kings and why a king's greeting is doubled, and he gave a verse for each. When they invited him to eat, he quoted Rav's teaching that a person may not taste anything before feeding his animal.
why: The Gemara has been discussing Rav's rule that one does not double the greeting of peace to a gentile; Geneiva's doubled greeting to the Sages shows when doubling is proper and where it comes from.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: One of the two Sages Geneiva greets.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: One of the two Sages Geneiva greets.

people.name: Geneiva
people.about: A Sage whom one of the pair calls a son of Torah and the other calls argumentative.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Geneiva quotes his teachings, which he reports in Rav's name.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The authority behind the teachings Geneiva quotes.

terms.meaning: Saying "peace" twice. Geneiva learns from a verse where David is greeted "peace, peace be to you" that a king is greeted this way.

note: A man sent a bill of divorce to his wife by an agent. The agent found her kneading dough and told her to take it; she said, "Let it be in your hand." Rav Nahman said that if the law follows Rabbi Hanina, he would rule the divorce valid, but Rava objected that the husband's agent had not finished his task, so the wife could not make him her agent. They sent the question to Rabbi Ami, who said the divorce was not valid, while Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba asked for time; when they asked him again he said the matter was as uncertain to him as to them.
why: The Gemara is debating whether a wife can appoint an agent to receive her bill of divorce from her husband's agent. The case is left unsettled, and the Gemara goes on to treat the woman as possibly married and possibly divorced.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Says he would rule the divorce valid if the law follows Rabbi Hanina.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Objects that the husband's agent never completed his task.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Rules that the divorce does not take effect.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: Asked twice; finally says the question is as uncertain to him as to those asking.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: His view, that a wife can appoint such an agent, is the question in the case.

terms.meaning: The document (in Hebrew, a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage. It can be delivered by an agent, and a wife can also appoint an agent to receive it.

note: A husband told witnesses to write a bill of divorce for his wife, whose name was Nefata, but they wrote Tefata by mistake. Rav Yitzhak bar Shmuel bar Marta ruled in Rav's name that the document was invalid because of the wrong name, but that the witnesses could not write a new one, since they had already carried out their task.
why: Rabba and then Rav Nahman go on to object to this ruling, debating when witnesses who wrote a bill of divorce have finished their agency and when they may write another.

people.name: Nefata
people.about: The woman being divorced; the witnesses wrote her name wrongly as Tefata.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Shmuel bar Marta
people.about: Rules on the case in the name of Rav.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The authority in whose name the ruling is given.

terms.meaning: The document (in Hebrew, a get) that ends a marriage; it must name the wife correctly.
Finished the job they were appointed to do, so their authority to act for the husband is over.

note: Geneiva was being led out in a neck chain to be executed. As he went, he said: "Give four hundred dinars to Rabbi Avina from my wine in Nehar Panya." Rabbi Zeira said that Rabbi Avina should lift his basket and go to his teacher Rav Huna, who taught that a man's bill of divorce has the same status as his gift.
why: The mishna says a man led out to execution who says "Write a bill of divorce for my wife" is understood to mean that it should also be given to her. Rabbi Zeira ties this to Geneiva's dying gift through Rav Huna's teaching that the two are treated alike.

people.name: Geneiva
people.about: A man led out to be executed who leaves money to Rabbi Avina.

people.name: Rabbi Avina
people.about: The man Geneiva leaves the four hundred dinars to.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Says Rabbi Avina can collect the gift by relying on his teacher Rav Huna.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Rabbi Avina's teacher, who compared a deathbed bill of divorce to a deathbed gift.

terms.meaning: A collar placed on a condemned man being taken out to be executed.
A silver coin.

note: A man walked into a synagogue and found a schoolteacher, the teacher's son, and another man sitting there. He told them, "Two of you should write a bill of divorce for my wife." The schoolteacher then died, and the question arose whether the son and the other man could write it. Rav Nahman said people do not appoint a son as agent in his father's place; Rav Pappi said they do; Rava ruled that they do.
why: The Gemara is discussing when a husband's spoken instruction to write a bill of divorce is enough to act on; this case asks who exactly he appointed when he said "two of you."

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Holds that the son cannot step in for his father.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: Holds that the son can step in for his father.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules that the son can step in.

terms.meaning: Someone appointed to act for another person, here to write and deliver a bill of divorce. A father and son cannot serve together as witnesses because they are relatives.

note: Shmuel reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled the law follows Rabbi Yosei, who says spoken instructions cannot be handed on to an agent. His son, Rabbi Shimon, asked why, since Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Hanina of Ono disagree with Rabbi Yosei. His father told him: "Be silent, my son, be silent. You did not see Rabbi Yosei; if you had, you would know that his reasoning goes with his statements."
why: The Gemara has been working out where Shmuel follows Rabbi Yosei on passing a husband's instructions to another agent; this exchange gives the ruling Shmuel relies on, and a baraita follows describing Rabbi Yosei and other Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Rules the law follows Rabbi Yosei and defends it to his son.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who questions the ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage whose opinion is accepted; his reasoning goes with his statements.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Reports Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Disagrees with Rabbi Yosei, along with Rabbi Hanina of Ono.

terms.meaning: An instruction someone only spoke (such as a husband telling people to write a bill of divorce) cannot be passed on by them to a further agent.

note: The members of the Exilarch's house would torment Rav Amram the pious by making him lie all night on the snow. The next day they would ask what he wanted to eat. Knowing they would do the opposite of whatever he said, he asked for red meat roasted over coals and diluted wine, and they brought him fatty meat and undiluted wine, which is what he wanted. Yalta, Rav Nahman's wife, heard about it and took him to the bathhouse, keeping him in the water until it turned red like blood and his flesh was covered with coin-like spots.
why: The Gemara has just given remedies: red roasted meat with diluted wine for fever, fatty roasted meat with undiluted wine for chills. Rav Amram uses that very knowledge to get the cure for chills.

people.name: Rav Amram the pious
people.about: A Sage tormented by the Exilarch's household.

people.name: Yalta
people.about: Rav Nahman's wife, who takes Rav Amram to the bathhouse.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia; his household and servants appear here.

note: The Exilarch asked Rav Sheshet, who was blind, why he would not eat with him. Rav Sheshet said the servants were suspected of eating flesh cut from a living animal, and proved it: his servant stole a leg from a slaughtered animal, the servants then brought three legs, cut a leg from a living animal to make four, and the stolen one made five. At the meal the servants hid a small bone in his meat to choke him, so he wrapped the meat in his scarf; they then claimed a silver cup was stolen, found the meat, and said he wanted only to shame them, but he said it had a leprous spot, and on checking it did. As he left they covered a pit with a mat; Rav Hisda snorted to warn him, a child recited "Turn to your right or to your left," and he went around it.
why: It continues the Gemara's run of stories about Sages and the house of the Exilarch, following the story of Rav Amram, whom the Exilarch's household tormented.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A blind Sage who will not eat at the Exilarch's table and sees through the servants' tricks.

people.name: Exilarch
people.about: The leader whose servants Rav Sheshet suspects.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Present at the end; snorts to warn Rav Sheshet of the pit and asks how he knew.

terms.meaning: Flesh cut from an animal while it is still alive, which Jewish law forbids eating.
The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.
Rav Sheshet quotes Rav Hisda that black spots on white skin or white spots on black skin are a sign of disease in the animal.

note: A remedy for intestinal pain is to take three hundred long peppers and drink a hundred of them in wine each day. Ravin of Neresh prepared a hundred and fifty of the local peppers in this way for the daughter of Rav Ashi, and she was healed.
why: It comes in a long list of remedies the Gemara gives for illnesses; this one carries a report of it being used.

people.name: Ravin of Neresh
people.about: Prepares the pepper remedy for Rav Ashi's daughter.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: His daughter is healed by the remedy.

note: For an illness of the spleen, one remedy is to roast a fish in a blacksmith's shop, eat it with the water used there to cool the hot metal, and drink that water. As evidence, the Gemara tells of a goat that used to drink water at a blacksmith's shop; when it was slaughtered, no spleen was found inside it.
why: It comes in the Gemara's list of remedies for an illness of the spleen, as evidence that the blacksmith's water works.

note: A remedy for a skin disease called lichen is to roast seven large wheat kernels on the blade of a new hoe, extract their oil and rub it on the skin. Rav Shimi bar Ashi used this remedy on a gentile who had "something else," which the translation explains as leprosy, and he was healed.
why: It comes in a long list of remedies the Gemara gives for illnesses; this one carries a report of it being used.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Ashi
people.about: Uses the remedy to heal a gentile.

note: Abaye said that someone who does the six exhausting acts just listed in that order dies, and someone who does them out of order becomes weak. The Gemara objects that a woman named Me'oret made her slave do three of them and he died. The Gemara answers that that slave was weak.
why: The Gemara has just listed six acts that kill a person if done one after another; Me'oret's slave is brought as a challenge to Abaye's claim that doing them out of order only weakens him.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Says the six acts kill only when done in order.

people.name: Me'oret
people.about: A woman who made her slave perform three of the acts.

note: When Rabba bar Avuh was ill, Rav Huna and Rav Nahman went to visit him. Rav Huna told Rav Nahman to ask him whether the law follows Rabbi Yosei; Rav Nahman said he did not even know Rabbi Yosei's reason, and Rav Huna promised to tell him afterward. Rabba bar Avuh answered in Rav's name that the law does follow Rabbi Yosei. After they left, Rav Huna explained Rabbi Yosei's reason: the date written in a document proves when it takes effect.
why: The Gemara is asking whether Rav Huna was uncertain about following Rabbi Yosei. This visit shows he accepted Rabbi Yosei's view, so the Gemara concludes he was unsure only whether it applies when the husband adds a spoken condition.

people.name: Rabba bar Avuh
people.about: An ill Sage asked for the ruling; he answers in Rav's name.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Wants the ruling and explains Rabbi Yosei's reason afterward.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Asks the question at Rav Huna's request.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage whose opinion is in question.

terms.term: The date of a document proves
terms.meaning: Rabbi Yosei's principle that the date written on a document shows it takes effect from that day, even if this is not stated explicitly.

note: A man sold land and took on responsibility for any accident that might happen to it; then a river was diverted through it. The buyer came before Ravina, who told the seller to pay, but Rav Aha bar Tahalifa said this was an uncommon accident. The case reached Rava, who agreed it was uncommon. Ravina raised a teaching about a bill of divorce against him, Rava answered that the same teaching points the other way in its first clause, and in the end Ravina told Rav Aha of Difti that the teaching was corrupt and one must follow reason.
why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching on a bill of divorce conditioned on dying of an illness, where the house collapsed or a snake bit. This sale case tests whether such a condition covers rare accidents, using that same teaching.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: First rules the seller must pay, later accepts that a rare accident is not covered.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Tahalifa
people.about: Objects that a river diverted through land is an uncommon accident.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules it an uncommon accident and answers Ravina's objection.

people.name: Rav Aha of Difti
people.about: Asks Ravina whether the teaching can still be used as an objection.

terms.meaning: Damage or loss no one could prevent. The question is whether a promise to cover "any accident" includes rare ones.
A teaching from the time of the mishna that was not included in the mishna itself.

note: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, bought sesame on the bank of the Malka River and hired sailors to carry it across, who took on responsibility for any accident. Then the river was dammed. The two Sages told the sailors to hire donkeys and bring the sesame, but when they came before Rava he called them "white geese who strip people of their cloaks" and said this was an uncommon accident.
why: The Gemara has just concluded that a promise to cover any accident does not include rare ones; this case applies that conclusion.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: One of the two Sages who bought the sesame.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Rav Pappa's partner in buying the sesame.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge, who rules against the two Sages.

terms.meaning: Rava's insult for the two Sages; the translation says it refers to their long white beards.

note: A landowner told his sharecropper: everyone else waters a field three times and takes a quarter of the crop; you water it four times and take a third. In the end rain fell, so the fourth watering was not needed. Rav Yosef said he did not water a fourth time, so he gets only a quarter; Rabba said the fourth watering was not needed, so he gets a third.
why: The Gemara is discussing whether a condition must be carried out exactly or only in its purpose, as with a bill of divorce given on a condition. It asks whether Rav Yosef and Rabba follow the two sides of that dispute, and concludes that both follow the Rabbis.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Rules the sharecropper gets only a quarter.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Rules the sharecropper gets a third.

terms.meaning: A farmer who works another person's field in return for a share of the crop.

note: A teaching reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: "After the Festival" means thirty days after it. Rabbi Hiyya went out and taught this in public in his name, and the people praised it; when he taught it as the view of the majority, they did not praise it.
why: The Gemara is working out how long time phrases like "after a year" or "after a week" mean in a conditional bill of divorce. It concludes from the reaction that the law does not follow this view.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The Sage who taught that after the Festival means thirty days.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Teaches the ruling in public, first in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's name and then as the majority view.

terms.meaning: One of the pilgrimage festivals of the Jewish year.

note: A man on his deathbed wrote a bill of divorce for his wife as Shabbat was approaching, but did not manage to hand it to her, and the next day his condition grew worse. People came to Rava, who told them: have him transfer to her the spot where the document is lying, and let her close and open the door there to take possession of it, and the document with it. Rav Ilish objected that whatever a wife acquires belongs to her husband, and Rava was embarrassed. In the end it emerged that she was only betrothed, not married. Rava said the rule about a married woman would not apply to a betrothed one, and then ruled that for either kind of wife, her bill of divorce and her courtyard reach her at the same moment.
why: The discussion is about whether a woman's own courtyard can receive her bill of divorce, given her husband's rights in her property. The Gemara then says Rava first stated his principle that the divorce and the courtyard arrive together in connection with this incident.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage asked what to do; his ruling is challenged and he then restates it.

people.name: Rav Ilish
people.about: Challenges Rava, pointing out that what a wife acquires belongs to her husband.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage. The divorce takes effect when it reaches her hand or her property.
A woman in the first stage of Jewish marriage: legally bound to her husband but not yet living with him as his wife.
A formal act, such as locking, fencing or breaching a wall, by which a person acquires land. The mishna quoted lists these.

note: A man threw a bill of divorce to his wife while she was standing in a courtyard, and it landed on a wooden board. Rav Yosef said they must look at the board's size: if it measured four cubits by four cubits it counts as a separate area of its own, and she is not divorced; if it was smaller, it is all one area with the courtyard, and she is divorced.
why: The Gemara has been asking how a courtyard can receive a bill of divorce for a woman. It then works out that the case must be one where the husband lent her his courtyard, since a loan covers one area, not a second one.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who rules on where the bill of divorce landed.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage; it takes effect when it reaches her hand or a place that acquires for her.
A measure of length, roughly the distance from elbow to fingertip. Four cubits by four is the size at which an area counts as a place of its own.
An area treated as a single place in law. Whether the board is its own domain or part of the courtyard decides whether the document reached her.

note: After Rabbi Eliezer died, four Sages came forward to refute his ruling on a divorce that leaves the woman free to marry anyone except one named man. Rabbi Tarfon argued that such a divorce could cancel a Torah law, the duty of levirate marriage. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili said that what is forbidden is forbidden to everyone. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya said a document of severance must sever the bond completely. Rabbi Akiva argued that it could void the divorce and make her later children mamzerim, and that she would count as a widow to one priest and a divorcee to everyone else. Each ended: this is not severance. Rabbi Yehoshua told them that one does not refute a lion after his death.
why: The Gemara has been exploring a husband's stipulation that forbids his ex-wife one man. Afterward Rava says every one of these refutations can itself be answered except Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's, and the Gemara goes through them one by one.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage, now dead, whose ruling the others set out to refute.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: Argues the stipulation could uproot the law of levirate marriage.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Argues from the Torah's word for divorce, severance.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Gives two arguments: void divorces and children who would be mamzerim, and the case of a priest.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Tells the others not to refute a great Sage who can no longer answer.

terms.meaning: When a man dies childless, his brother marries the widow. A stipulation forbidding her to that brother would block this Torah duty.
The Torah calls a bill of divorce a scroll of severance; the argument is that it must cut every tie between husband and wife.
Plural of mamzer: a child born of a forbidden union such as adultery, who is barred from marrying most Jews.
An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one: if the lesser prohibition applies, the greater one surely does.

note: A rumor spread that a certain woman had been betrothed to a Torah student. Rav Hama summoned her father and asked him exactly what had happened. The father said the student had betrothed her on condition that he would not go to Bei Hozai, and then he went, so the betrothal was void. Rav Hama answered that since this explanation did not exist when the rumor spread, the father could not now create it, and the rumor had to be taken seriously.
why: Abaye and Rav Yosef have just argued over whether a court sets aside an unconfirmed rumor that a woman is betrothed; Rav Yosef says places differ. This is the first of several such cases the Gemara brings, and here the rumor is not set aside.

people.name: Rav Ḥama
people.about: The Sage who questions the woman's father and rules on the rumor.

terms.meaning: Betrothal is the first, legally binding stage of Jewish marriage. A rumor that a woman is betrothed could stop her marrying anyone else.
A betrothal made on a stated condition; if the condition is broken, the betrothal never took effect.

note: A rumor spread that a certain woman had been betrothed with a mat of dates from the spring of Bei Shifei. Rav Idi bar Avin sent the case to Abaye, asking what to do. Abaye answered that even those who say a rumor is not set aside would set this one aside: if she marries someone else, people will not slander her, but will say the Sages looked into the betrothal and found the mat was not worth a peruta.
why: The Gemara is debating whether a court sets aside a rumor that a woman is betrothed, and brings a series of cases. This one shows Abaye making an exception even under the strict view, because the rumor itself points to an invalid betrothal.

people.name: Rav Idi bar Avin
people.about: Sends the case to Abaye for a ruling.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rules that this rumor is set aside.

terms.meaning: The smallest coin. A betrothal must be made with something worth at least a peruta, or it does not take effect.
To disregard a rumor that a woman is betrothed, so that she may marry someone else.

note: A rumor spread that a certain woman had been betrothed to a boy who was still a minor but looked like an adult. Rav Mordekhai told Rav Ashi there had already been such a case, and the Sages said the boy had not yet reached the divisions of Reuben, a phrase from the book of Judges about maturity of heart, so the betrothal counted for nothing.
why: This closes the Gemara's series of cases on whether a rumor of betrothal is set aside. The Gemara then turns to the mishna's rule that a rumor counts only when there is no explanation for it.

people.name: Rav Mordekhai
people.about: Tells Rav Ashi of an earlier case like this one.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage to whom the precedent is reported.

terms.meaning: A child below the age of legal adulthood. A minor boy cannot make a valid betrothal, however grown he looks.
Words from Judges 5:16, read here to mean the maturity of mind that comes with adulthood.
